# Growth variability and life-history priors

## CVL

`CVL` is the coefficient of variation of Linf among growth-type groups. It sets how
far individual growth spreads the length composition, mostly in the tail: the
fastest-growing groups determine how many fish occur near and beyond Linf. It is
fixed at its input value unless `CVL.sd` is given; typical values are 0.07-0.15.

The sensitivity below refits the model for three CVL values (`cvl_values`),
without and with a tail cut at 47 cm; `Map()` runs one fit per value.

```{r cvl-sens, fig.height = 4}
cvl_values <- c(0.07, 0.10, 0.13)

fits_cvl <- Map(function(cvl) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = cvl, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating"), se = FALSE)
}, cvl_values)
names(fits_cvl) <- paste0("CVL_", cvl_values)

fits_cvl_cut <- Map(function(cvl) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = cvl, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", tail_cut = 47), se = FALSE)
}, cvl_values)
names(fits_cvl_cut) <- paste0("CVL_", cvl_values, "_cut47")

cvl_table <- data.frame(CVL       = cvl_values,
                        SPR_no_cut = round(sapply(fits_cvl, sprcur_flicc), 3),
                        SPR_cut47  = round(sapply(fits_cvl_cut, sprcur_flicc), 3),
                        row.names = NULL)
cvl_table
plot_spr(c(fits_cvl, fits_cvl_cut))
```

Status is sensitive to CVL because CVL shapes the tail: here SPR ranges
`r min(cvl_table$SPR_no_cut)`-`r max(cvl_table$SPR_no_cut)` over CVL 0.07-0.13
without a cut and `r min(cvl_table$SPR_cut47)`-`r max(cvl_table$SPR_cut47)` with a
cut at 47 cm.

## maxsd and ngtg

The growth groups are placed at $z_h$ on `seq(-maxsd, maxsd, length = ngtg)` with
normal weights. Truncating the normal at `maxsd` reduces the realised CV of the
groups below CVL and caps the largest group at $L_\infty(1 + \text{maxsd}\cdot\text{CVL})$:

The realised spread can be computed directly from the group positions `z` and
their normal weights `w`; the factor multiplies CVL:

```{r maxsd-cv}
z <- seq(-2, 2, length.out = 13)          # maxsd = 2, ngtg = 13 (LBSPR)
w <- dnorm(z) / sum(dnorm(z))
sqrt(sum(w * z^2))                        # realised CV factor

z <- seq(-3, 3, length.out = 13)          # maxsd = 3, ngtg = 13 (default)
w <- dnorm(z) / sum(dnorm(z))
sqrt(sum(w * z^2))

55.7 * (1 + c(2, 3) * 0.1)                # largest group Linf for maxsd 2 and 3
```

With the LBSPR default (`maxsd = 2`, 13 groups) the realised CV is about 0.9 x
CVL; `maxsd = 3` gives almost exactly CVL and allows larger fish. The number of
groups matters little beyond about 13, and computing time grows with it.

The fits below compare LBSPR's grid with the default and a finer grid
(`maxsd_values` with matching `ngtg_values`), without and with the tail cut; `Map()` takes the two vectors in
parallel.

```{r maxsd-sens}
maxsd_values <- c(2, 3, 3)
ngtg_values  <- c(13, 13, 19)

fits_maxsd <- Map(function(maxsd, ngtg) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", maxsd = maxsd, ngtg = ngtg), se = FALSE)
}, maxsd_values, ngtg_values)

fits_maxsd_cut <- Map(function(maxsd, ngtg) {
  fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
         settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating", maxsd = maxsd, ngtg = ngtg,
                         tail_cut = 47), se = FALSE)
}, maxsd_values, ngtg_values)

data.frame(maxsd      = maxsd_values,
           ngtg       = ngtg_values,
           SPR_no_cut = round(sapply(fits_maxsd, sprcur_flicc), 3),
           SPR_cut47  = round(sapply(fits_maxsd_cut, sprcur_flicc), 3))
```

The default is `maxsd = 3, ngtg = 13` (from FLicc 1.0.11; before: LBSPR's
`maxsd = 2, ngtg = 13`); 19 groups give the same result at about 25% more
computing time. With `maxsd = 2` the largest group is
$1.2 L_\infty$ at CVL = 0.1, and fish above it get a near-zero probability:
each such fish costs about the same in the likelihood. In sensitivity runs
and Monte Carlo draws with a lower Linf or CVL, this gives steps in the AIC
and failed refits. `maxsd = 3` extends the groups to $1.3 L_\infty$, and CVL
is then close to the realised spread, which matters when CVL is taken from
external growth studies (with `maxsd = 2`, a CVL input of 0.1 corresponds to
a realised spread of about 0.09). At the input life history the two settings
usually give similar results. Use `maxsd = 2` to reproduce LBSPR.

## Estimating Linf, M/k and CVL with priors

By default growth and natural mortality are fixed. `linf.sd`, `Mk.sd` and
`CVL.sd` estimate them with normal priors on the log scale around the inputs:
$$
\log L_\infty \sim N(\log L_\infty^{in}, \texttt{linf.sd}^2), \quad
\log (M/k) \sim N(\log (M/k)^{in}, \texttt{Mk.sd}^2), \quad
\log \mathrm{CVL} \sim N(\log \mathrm{CVL}^{in}, \texttt{CVL.sd}^2),
$$
so each sd is approximately a CV (e.g. `linf.sd = 0.05`: about ±10% at 95%).

The fit below estimates all three with priors. The estimates are on the log
scale: $L_\infty$ = `exp(log_Linf)`, $M/k$ = `exp(log_Mk)` and CVL =
`1 / sqrt(exp(log_Galpha))`; the column `se` is approximately the posterior CV
(for `log_Galpha` divide by 2).

```{r priors, fig.height = 4}
fit_pri <- fiticc(lfd, stklen, sel_fun = sel_fun, catch_by_gear = cbg,
                  settings = list(CVL = 0.1, obs_model = "dm", dm_theta = "saturating",
                                  linf.sd = 0.05, Mk.sd = 0.1, CVL.sd = 0.25))

est <- fit_pri$par[fit_pri$par$par %in% c("log_Linf", "log_Mk", "log_Galpha"), ]
est
exp(est$mpd[est$par == "log_Linf"])            # Linf (input 55.7)
exp(est$mpd[est$par == "log_Mk"])              # M/k  (input 0.162 / 0.08 = 2.03)
1 / sqrt(exp(est$mpd[est$par == "log_Galpha"])) # CVL  (input 0.1)

plot_spr(list(fixed = fit, priors = fit_pri), ci = TRUE)
```

```{r priors-numbers, include = FALSE}
pp <- function(nm, col = "mpd") est[[col]][est$par == nm][1]
```

Here the length data pull Linf up to about `r round(exp(pp("log_Linf")), 1)`
(posterior CV `r round(pp("log_Linf", "se"), 3)` against a prior CV of 0.05), and
because a larger Linf means the fish in the catch are relatively younger, SPR
drops markedly. The posterior CVs of M/k and CVL stay close to their prior CVs:
the data say little about them. A shift of this size in Linf is a finding to
check against growth studies, not a result to accept; run the assessment with
Linf fixed at the alternative values as a sensitivity.

Notes:

- **k** is not estimated separately: the length model depends on M/k (and Z/k), so
  uncertainty in k and M is expressed through `Mk.sd`. k still sets the time scale
  of the annual F estimates (F is estimated as F/k).
- Length data carry limited information on Linf and CVL, and both are confounded
  with dome-shaped selectivity and the tail; a posterior CV close to the prior CV
  means the data are uninformative. Large moves away from the input (several prior
  SDs) indicate a conflict between the data and the life history, to be
  investigated rather than accepted.
- For ensembles, drawing the life-history parameters and keeping them fixed in
  each fit (`mc_flicc()`) is usually better behaved than estimating them.
